prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You love a woman and you wonder where she goes all night in some tricked- out taxicab, with her high heels and her corset and her big, fat mouth. You love how she only wears her glasses with you, how thick and cow-eyed she swears it’s only ever you she wants to see. You love her, you want her very ugly. If she is lovely big, you want her scrawny. If she is perfect lithe, you want her ballooned, a cosmonaut. How not to love her, her bouillabaisse, her orangina. When you took her to the doctor the doctor said, “Wow, look at that!” and you were proud, you asshole, you love and that’s how you are in love. Any expert, observing human bodies, can see how she’s exceptional, how she ruins us all. But you really love this woman, how come no one can see this? Everyone must become suddenly very clumsy at recognizing beauty if you are to keep her. You don’t want to lose anything, at all, ever. You want her sex depilated, you want everyone else not blind, but perhaps paralyzed, from the eyes down. You wonder where she goes all night. If she leaves you, you will know everything about love. If she’s leaving you now, you already know it.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, How, When

outputs.L1: You love a woman, and you wonder where she disappears to all night in some gaudy, tricked-out taxicab, with her high heels and her corset and her big, brazen mouth. You love that she wears her glasses only for you—how earnestly, with those thick lenses and wide, cow-eyed devotion, she swears it is only ever you she wishes to see. You love her; you want her at her most unlovely. If she is voluptuous, you want her gaunt. If she is flawlessly lithe, you want her swollen and ungainly, a cosmonaut. How could one not love her—her bouillabaisse, her orangina? When you took her to the doctor, the doctor exclaimed, "Wow, look at that!" and you swelled with pride, you fool—you love, and that is how you are in love. Any expert, surveying the human form, can see how exceptional she is, how utterly she undoes us all. Yet you truly love this woman—why can no one else perceive it? Everyone must suddenly grow hopelessly inept at recognizing beauty if you are to keep her. You do not want to lose anything, ever, at all. You want her sex depilated; you want everyone else not blind, but perhaps paralyzed, from the eyes down. You wonder where she goes all night. If she leaves you, you will come to understand everything about love. If she is leaving you now, then you already do.
outputs.L2: There's a woman you're devoted to, and it eats at you—wondering where she vanishes to each night in some souped-up cab, dressed in her stilettos and her corset, running that loud mouth of hers. It thrills you that she puts on her glasses only when she's with you, that she promises, wide-eyed and earnest, that you're the only thing she ever cares to look at. You love her, and you want her hideous. Should she be gorgeously full-figured, you'd wish her bony instead. Were she flawlessly slender, you'd want her bloated up like an astronaut. How could anyone not adore her—her stew, her fizzy drink. That time you brought her to the doctor's office, the physician exclaimed, "Wow, would you look at that!" and it filled you with pride, you jerk—this is what your loving amounts to, this is your version of being in love. Put any specialist in front of a room of human forms and they'd spot instantly how rare she is, how she leaves the rest of us in ruins. Yet you genuinely love this woman—why can't a single soul recognize it? For you to hold onto her, the whole world would need to lose its ability to notice loveliness overnight. You refuse to surrender a thing, not now, not ever. You want her sex stripped bare, you want everyone else not sightless exactly, but maybe frozen stiff from the eyes on down. And still you wonder where she disappears to at night. Should she ever walk away, you'll finally grasp everything there is to know about love. And if she's walking away this very moment, then you already understand it.
outputs.L3:
# An Obsessive Love

I love her with a desperation that borders on madness, yet even in the depths of my devotion I am tormented by suspicion. Where does she go when night falls? What draws her away into the darkness, hour after hour, until dawn? I cannot say, and it is this not knowing that consumes me. My love and my mistrust have grown together, tangled beyond separation, so that I can no longer tell where affection ends and jealousy begins.

My desire for her is riddled with contradiction. There are moments when I wish she were ugly, misshapen, marked by some visible flaw—anything to make her less desirable to the world. If she were imperfect, perhaps I could love her in peace. Her beauty, which should be my greatest joy, becomes instead the source of my deepest anguish, for it belongs not only to me but to every eye that falls upon her.

I take pride in her exceptional loveliness. When others turn to look at her, some part of me swells with satisfaction, knowing that she is mine. Yet in the same instant that pride curdles into resentment. Every admiring glance feels like a theft, every appreciative word a small betrayal. I cannot enjoy her beauty without being poisoned by the awareness that others enjoy it too.

What I truly want is impossible: I wish that everyone else were blind to her charm, incapable of perceiving what I perceive. Let her radiance be visible to me alone. Let the whole world look upon her and see nothing worth desiring, so that I might keep her entirely to myself, hoarded like a secret treasure that no one else can appreciate or covet.

And in this possessive terror—this desperate fear of losing her—lies a truth I am only beginning to understand. Perhaps I will never truly comprehend the nature of my love until the moment she leaves me. Only in her absence, when she is finally beyond my grasp, will I grasp at last what she meant, and what love itself demanded of me all along.
outputs.L4:
# The Shape of You in Absence

You are the thought I cannot finish and cannot abandon. You occupy me the way water occupies a glass—completely, taking the shape of whatever holds you, indifferent to the vessel. I want to possess you and I want you free; I want you to belong to me and I want you to have never needed belonging at all. Do you see the impossibility I have made of myself? I have built a house with two doors and locked them both from the inside.

When you laugh at something someone else has said, I feel the laughter as a small theft. Not of you, exactly, but of the version of you I had convinced myself was mine alone—the one who laughs only in my kitchen, only at my clumsiness, only in the dim gold of our particular evenings. I know this is madness. I know you are not a coin I can keep in a closed fist. And yet the fist closes anyway, involuntary, a reflex older than reason.

I want to know everything about you and I want there to be a room in you I can never enter, because the mystery is what I love and the knowing is what I need. See how I contradict myself in a single breath. I want you predictable enough to trust and unpredictable enough to worship. I want to be the center of your world and I resent that you have made me one, because now I am afraid of the edges, of what lies beyond me, of the whole vast geography of your life that does not include me.

Here is a hand on your shoulder that is not mine. Here is a message on your phone I did not send. Here is the small crease between your eyebrows when you read something private, and I invent a hundred stories to fill that crease, each of them a knife I have made and then pressed against my own throat. Jealousy is not about you. I understand this now. It is a mirror in which I see only my own insufficiency, my own certainty that I am not enough to hold you, that I was never enough, that love is a debt I can never fully repay.

And so I hoard you. I count your glances the way a miser counts coins in the dark, never spending, never trusting, terrified that the treasure will vanish the moment I look away. But treasure guarded too closely becomes a prison for the one who guards it. I have made myself the jailer and the prisoner both.

It was only when you left—only in the raw architecture of your absence—that I finally understood what I had been holding. Now the apartment keeps your shape: your coat's ghost on the hook, the particular silence where your voice used to be, the cold half of the bed that I cannot bring myself to warm. And in this loss, this unbearable clarity, I see that I never truly saw you until you were gone. My love, so certain of itself, was blind. It took you until now to become real.

This is the cruel paradox, the one I would not learn any other way: I did not know the weight of what I carried until my arms were empty. I did not understand the depth of my attachment until there was nothing left to attach to but the memory of your leaving. I loved you all along, yes—but I only *knew* it in the moment I could no longer prove it to you.

You are the thought I cannot finish. You are the door I locked from the inside, and now I stand outside it, in the rain, understanding at last what a fool does with the thing he fears to lose. He loses it. And only then does he learn, too late, exactly what it was worth.
outputs.L5:
# You, How, and When: The Three Pillars of Meaningful Change

Every significant transformation in life comes down to answering three simple yet profound questions: **who** you are, **how** you will act, and **when** you will begin. Understanding these elements can turn vague dreams into concrete achievements.

## You: The Starting Point

Everything begins with **you**. Before setting goals or making plans, it's essential to understand your own values, strengths, and limitations. You are the driving force behind every decision you make. When you take ownership of your choices, you stop waiting for circumstances to align perfectly and start creating opportunities for yourself. Self-awareness isn't about being self-critical—it's about knowing exactly what you want and why it matters to you.

## How: The Method Matters

Once you know what you want, the next challenge is figuring out **how** to get there. Good intentions rarely succeed without a clear strategy. How you approach a problem often determines whether you overcome it. Will you break a large goal into smaller steps? How will you handle setbacks when they inevitably appear? The "how" is where discipline meets creativity, transforming abstract wishes into actionable plans.

## When: The Power of Timing

Finally, there is the question of **when**. Timing can make the difference between success and missed opportunity. Many people delay action, telling themselves they'll start "someday" or "when the time is right." But the truth is, the perfect moment rarely arrives on its own. When you commit to a specific time—today, this week, this month—you give your goals the urgency they need to become reality.

## Bringing It All Together

**You** provide the purpose. **How** provides the path. **When** provides the momentum. When these three elements work in harmony, change stops feeling overwhelming and starts feeling possible. So ask yourself: Who are you trying to become, how will you get there, and when will you take the first step?

The answers are already within you—all that remains is the courage to act.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem in second person about obsessive, jealous love, addressing a "you" who loves a woman and wonders where she goes all night.
counterfactuals.output:
# Nocturne for the Sleepless

You lie awake counting the ways a door can close. She left at nine, and now the clock has become a thing with teeth, gnawing the hours between her leaving and your certainty that she will not return. You have memorized the sound of her key, the particular hesitation before the lock turns, and tonight you listen for it the way a drowning man listens for the shore.

Where does she go, you wonder, and the wondering is a country you have built for yourself, a small nation of one, its borders drawn in the salt of what you cannot know. You imagine her laughter belonging to someone else. You imagine the light in a bar falling on her face the way your hands used to. Every stranger becomes a suspect. Every silence, a confession.

You have started to love her the way frost loves the window—clinging, obscuring, turning the clear glass opaque with your breath. You tell yourself this is devotion. You tell yourself the ache in your chest is proof of something pure, when it is only hunger wearing the mask of the sacred.

She comes home. She always comes home. And still you search her coat for the smell of another season, her phone for the names you don't recognize, her eyes for the door you're certain she's already walking through. You have made a prison and called it a heart. You have made a question with no answer and set it loose to devour you.

Ask yourself, in the blue hour before she wakes: what is it you love—her, or the wound she lets you keep?
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, intense piece about desire and possessiveness, using strange comparisons and a confessional tone. End with something about knowing everything about love if she leaves.
counterfactuals.output:
# What I Would Do

I want you the way a drowning man wants the specific weight of stone—not to be saved, but to be finished properly, to sink with something in my arms.

Let me confess. I have counted your teeth while you slept, all thirty-two of them, and I have named them after months so that your mouth contains an entire calendar I can live inside. When you yawn I feel the years passing. When you speak I lose track of time.

This is not normal. I know this is not normal.

You are a house with too many doors and I have tried to seal them all with my body, spread thin as wallpaper, pressed flat against your inner walls so that no draft, no other person, no stray idea of leaving can get through. I want to be the temperature you keep. I want to be the thing you cannot open a window against.

Desire, in me, has grown teeth of its own. It gnaws at the furniture. It has eaten through the floor. When you touch someone else's hand in passing I taste copper. When you laugh at a joke I did not make I feel myself becoming smaller, a coin swallowed by a machine that returns nothing, that only wants more coins, that hums with a hunger I have started to mistake for music.

I have kept your voicemails like pressed flowers. I have memorized the sound of your key. I could pick you out of a stampede by the rhythm of your particular panic.

Is this love? I have asked the mirror and the mirror, being honest, said nothing—just showed me a man holding his own throat like something he'd caught and didn't know how to release.

Here is the terrible arithmetic: the more I have of you, the less I trust that I have you. Possession is a bucket with no bottom. I pour you in and pour you in and stand there, forever thirsty, forever holding an empty and heavy thing.

And yet.

If you left—if you truly walked through one of those doors I forgot to seal, out into the ordinary weather where people go on breathing without me—I think, at last, I would understand it. All of it. The songs. The wars. The old men weeping at nothing.

Because you don't learn love while you're holding it.

You learn everything about love in the exact shape of the room after she's gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of experimental flash fiction exploring the ugliness of romantic obsession and the desire to control a partner's beauty so no one else notices her.
counterfactuals.output:
# Wax

He counts her eyelashes while she sleeps. Forty-one on the left. He knows because he pulls one out each night, so slowly her dreaming face never flinches, and drops it into the mason jar he keeps beneath the bed. The jar is nearly full. He tells himself he is collecting her. He is being *careful* with her. This is what love looks like when you do it correctly.

*

Listen. Here is what nobody admits.

When she laughs at the grocery store—too loud, too bright, that laugh like a window thrown open—the man stacking oranges *looks*. And something in me goes cold and surgical. I want to reach into her mouth and take the laugh out. Fold it small. Pocket it. Give it back to her at home where it belongs to me and only me.

*

She used to wear red.

Now she wears the colors I buy her. Gray, the color of weather that keeps people indoors. Brown, the color of being overlooked. I tell her it brings out her eyes. I do not tell her the truth, which is that I am building a fog around her, one cardigan at a time, so that when she walks down the street she disappears into the sidewalk and no one—

no one—

*

*Question:* If beauty is seen, and I prevent the seeing, have I destroyed the beauty or preserved it?

*Answer:* I have moved it into a room with no doors. I am the only one with a window. This is not a prison. I have simply made myself the *weather* through which she is glimpsed.

*

Some nights I imagine her face as a candle.

I love it best as it melts. Softening. Losing its edges. Becoming a thing that could not draw a stranger's eye because it no longer holds a shape worth turning toward. In the dream I am the flame *and* the hand cupped around the flame, and I am so gentle, I am so *loving*, as I watch the features I fell for run down into nothing.

I wake up. She is beside me, intact, luminous, unbearable.

I hate that she is beautiful.
I hate that others can see it.
I have confused these two sentences for the same sentence for so long that I no longer know which one is the wound and which one is the knife.

*

The jar holds forty-one nights.

This morning she stood at the mirror and said, *my lashes are so thin lately*, and touched the bare rim of her eye, and did not understand, and I felt it then—

the warm and rotten pleasure of it—

that I was winning.

That I was taking her out of the world one small piece at a time and calling it *devotion*.

*

Here is the ugliness. Not the wanting her. The wanting her *unwitnessed*. The way my love arrives already curdled, already a fist, already asking: *how do I make her smaller so she fits inside my fear?*

I do not want a wife.

I want a locked drawer that breathes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the style of a contemporary confessional poet about wanting to keep a lover all to yourself, full of jealousy, contradiction, and dark humor.
counterfactuals.output:
# Ways I Have Considered Keeping You

I want to fold you into my pocket
like a receipt for something
I can't afford but bought anyway,

want to introduce you to my friends
then take you home before
they realize how good you are at listening.

Here is my confession:
when you laugh at someone else's joke
I calculate the exact temperature of the room
and find it wanting.

I know this is not love,
or it is love wearing love's ugly cousin's coat,
the one with all the pockets
for keeping things.

You told me about your ex again
and I nodded like a good person
while a small animal in my chest
learned to bare its teeth.

I don't want to own you.
That's a lie. I do.
I want to be the only weather you check,
the single tab left open,
the last name you keep saying wrong
on purpose.

Isn't it funny—
I'd burn the whole village down
to keep you warm,
then blame you for the smoke,
then hold you while you cough.

Forgive me.
I'm working on it.
By working on it I mean
I've memorized the names
of everyone who's ever wanted you
and I whisper them at night
like a rosary,
like a hit list,
like a prayer
I'm too jealous
to finish.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a prose poem that captures the paradox of love and jealousy—wanting to possess someone completely, wishing others couldn't see how beautiful they are.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Locked Garden

I want to build walls around your beauty. There—I've said the ugly thing, the thing that lives beneath the tenderness like a root system, pale and grasping in the dark.

When you laugh in a crowded room, something in me curdles even as it soars. *Look how they look at you.* I am proud and poisoned in the same breath. I want the world to know I am loved by someone luminous, and I want to press my hand over that light, to be the only one warmed by it.

This is the arithmetic that doesn't work: I love you *because* you are beautiful to everyone, and I hate that you are beautiful to anyone but me. I want you seen and I want you invisible. I want to be generous with the ocean and I keep trying to carry it home in my cupped, leaking hands.

Tell me—when did devotion learn to wear the mask of ownership? When did *I cherish you* start to sound so much like *you are mine*?

I know the truth even as I resist it. A thing possessed completely is a thing that stops breathing. If I sealed you in my locked garden, I would have only a pressed flower—the shape of you, the memory of color, but none of the wild reaching-toward-sun that made me love you in the first place.

Your beauty was never mine to hoard. It was only ever mine to witness, alongside everyone else lucky enough to stand in the light you refuse to dim.

So I am learning to unclench. To let you be a window and not a mirror. To understand that the surest way to lose you is to grip too hard—and the only way to keep you is to hold you the way one holds water:

gently, gratefully, and with open hands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
